newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tokyo, Seoul shares nosedive on corporate fears.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo, Seoul shares nosedive on corporate fears.

text.p: Stock markets across most of Asia fell on Monday, led by sharp plunges in Tokyo and Seoul where fears of major corporate losses drove down shares.
Japanese stocks met a renewed selling, pushing the key market index 2.0 percent lower. The 225-share Nikkei average shed 354.46 points to close at 17,334.90, after briefly dipping to 17,280.20.
Brokers said rumours that a Japanese city bank had posted substantial losses in derivatives trading had reignited worries over the health of Japan's financial sector.
Sales of bank shares were triggered by a variety of vague rumours about new problems or possible derivatives losses in the banking industry, brokers said.
In Seoul, stocks fell sharply due to worries about the effects of the Hanbo Group's financial crisis, brokers said.
The composite index shed 2.98 percent, or 20.41 points, to close at a provisional 664.70.
"The issue is giving a renewed impact on the market as the case is seen spreading wider than earlier expected," said Jeon Jeong-tak of Hyundai Securities.
The nation's 14th-largest conglomerate is on the brink of a collapse after its flagship, Hanbo Steel Co, defaulted on debt repayments last Thursday.
President Kim Young-sam ordered a probe into the group while opposition parties alleged government complicity in what they called irregular loans to Hanbo Steel.
Hong Kong shares plunged in the afternoon on concerns about rising interest rates, and analysts said the downturn was likely to continue until a U.S. Federal Reserve meeting on February 4-5.
The Hang Seng Index fell 151 points, or 1.13 percent, to 13,228 in mid-afternoon.
"Hong Kong is just following what's happening in New York. It's likely to remain until after the Fed meeting," he added.
The U.S. index sank 59 points to 6696.48 on Friday, its third straight fall.

But stocks in Bombay bucked the trend. Mounting optimism about government announcements to shore up capital markets fuelled an early rally, sending the key share index surging 3.6 percent in hectic afternoon trade, dealers said.
At 12.22 p.m. (0652 GMT), the benchmark 30-share index of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) was up 123.88 points or 3.6 percent to 3,559.50.
In Taiwan, share prices were hit by a report of a possible tightening of money policy by the central bank, although the bank distanced itself from key elements of the report.
The weighted index ended 55.32 points or 0.77 percent lower at 7,156.96. Turnover was only T$48.9 billion, far below the T$100 billion-plus levels reached in many January sessions.

New Zealand shares eased slightly in quiet trading made more tranquil by holidays in Auckland and Australia. At the close the NZSE-40 capital index had dropped 0.29 percent to 2,393.25 as most leaders eased.
Shares in Singapore were weaker at noon with investors focused on speculative Malaysian over the counter stocks.
The Straits Times Industrials Index (STII) was down 0.47 percent to 2,232.17 at 0716 GMT.

In Bangkok, losses on Wall Street and some regional markets forced investors to sell some key issues, driving down the index by lunch. The SET index dropped 0.36 percent to 845.47 on thin 714 million baht turnover by the break.

"The market was very quiet this morning. My company received only a few phone calls from customers. Investors stayed out of the market due to declines in Wall Street and several Asian markets today," said a broker at a foreign brokerage house.
The Manila share index ended in negative territory as thirdliners continued to grab the spotlight from blue chips, traders said. The index fell 9.43 points, or 0.28 percent, to 3,323.10.
